sections.title: Neural networks, 1943–1986 · a static vector and a few categories
teaching: The vowel network summarizes networks from **1943 to 1986**, from **McCulloch and Pitts’s** logical calculus of all-or-none neurons to the 1986 **Parallel Distributed Processing** volumes. Given a **static vector** of formants, such a network decides among **a few categories**.
The problem is that **human cognition is far more complex**. Speech and language are sequences in time, and a network that maps one fixed vector to a few labels cannot represent what came before.

The caption also states the limit. **Human cognition is far more complex.** Speech unfolds in time, a sentence is a long sequence of words, and what comes next depends on what came before. A network that maps one fixed vector to a handful of labels has no way to represent a sequence or to keep track of earlier inputs.

To handle language, a network has to take in many vectors in order and use the earlier ones when it responds to the later ones. That requirement is what separates these classifiers from recurrent networks and, later, large language models.

sections.title: Jordan’s recurrent network for speech production
teaching: In **1985, Michael Jordan developed recurrent neural networks** to understand **speech production**, work that led toward **LLMs** and **agentic AI**. Output units loop back into **state units**, which also feed back to themselves, so each output depends on the **plan units** and the network’s own recent outputs.

The plot of **Performance on /istrstry/** traces eight articulatory features over 32 time steps. **Round** rises early and stays high, spreading across several sounds, and Sibilant peaks where the s sounds occur. The recurrence lets outputs blend smoothly over time.

The plot, **Performance on /istrstry/**, shows the network producing a sequence of sounds over time, from 0 to 32 time steps. Each row is one articulatory feature, **Voice, Place, Sonorant, Sibilant, Nasal, Height, Back and Round**, and each line gives how much of that feature the output has at each moment. Sibilant rises in bumps where the s sounds occur, while Nasal and Height stay nearly flat.

The **Round** line rises early and stays high for most of the sequence instead of switching on and off for single sounds. A feature spreads across neighboring sounds because the network’s outputs blend from one moment to the next. Producing a smooth, overlapping sequence like this is what a recurrent network adds to speech, and the same idea of feeding past outputs back in runs through to today’s language models.

sections.title: From one neuron to agentic systems
teaching: **One neuron** takes a vector and gives one number, an inner product. A **network** of weight layers W₁, W₂, W₃ turns a vector into a **decision vector**. An **LLM** takes **15 token vectors** up through **5 layers** of weights and returns **vector 16**, a probability distribution over the next token.

An **agentic system** is a **graph of LLMs**, Outline, Write, Critic, Revise and Final, with a **loop** between Critic and Revise. Underneath all of them, **inference is inner products** and **learning is SGD plus DP**.

The fourth column is an **agentic system, a graph of LLMs**. Separate LLMs are connected in order, **Outline, Write, Critic, Revise and Final**, with a **loop** between Critic and Revise. One model drafts, another critiques, another revises, and the critique can send the work back for more revision before the final model finishes. The parts are LLMs, and the system is the way they are wired together.

Under all four, the bottom line names what they share. **Inference is inner products**, weighted sums passed from layer to layer, whether in one neuron or in a large model. **Learning is SGD plus DP**, stochastic gradient descent guided by the dynamic-programming bookkeeping of backpropagation. The same two operations scale from the vowel classifier to an LLM.
concepts: agentic graph with a critic loop

sections.title: Fifteen vectors · the same next-item question for any sequence
teaching: An LLM receives **15 vectors** and predicts **x₁₆**. The vectors can be **15 words** of a sentence, **15 frames** of a spectrogram, **16 patches** of an image read row by row, or **15 amino acids** of the insulin B chain.

In each case x₁₆ is the next or missing piece, a word, a frame, a patch, or the residue Y. **The LLM only ever sees vectors**, so one machine answers one question for every kind of sequence, **what is x₁₆?**

The last example is a **protein, the insulin B chain**, read as **15 amino acids**, F V N Q H L C G S H L V E A L, drawn folding into a helix. Each amino acid is a vector, and **x₁₆ is the next residue**, which is **Y**. The same sixteenth slot sits at the end of every sequence.

The takeaway states the point of the four examples. **The LLM only ever sees vectors.** Words, sounds, pixels and molecules all become sequences of vectors, so **one machine asks one question, what is x₁₆?** Whatever the source, learning to predict the next vector in a sequence is the task the model is built for.

sections.title: Which sequences can be English words?
teaching: One-syllable words like Don, mat and fish follow a **consonant, vowel, consonant** pattern. Clusters are allowed **before and after the vowel** only in certain orders, so split, flat, desk and help are words while *sblit, *lfat, *desb and *hepl are impossible, with the order mirroring around the vowel.

A **long word is a chain of syllables**, each obeying the same rules. t·l is fine across a break in At·lan·tic, but **tl cannot start a syllable**, so *tlantic is impossible, and ng can end a syllable but never start one.

The third row has **words of many syllables**, with dots marking syllable breaks, such as **ba·na·na, win·dow, pump·kin, nap·kin, At·lan·tic, ath·lete, ad·mit and spa·ghet·ti**. Atlantic, athlete and admit contain t followed by l, th followed by l, and d followed by m. Those pairs are fine inside the word because a syllable break falls between them, but they cannot begin a word, so *tlantic, *thlete and *dmit are impossible. Likewise ng can end a syllable, as in ring, but never start one, so *ngapkin is impossible.

The rule for the whole page is that **a long word is a chain of syllables**, and every syllable obeys the same rules. **t·l is fine across a break, but tl cannot start a syllable.** This is **phonotactic knowledge**, the knowledge of which sound sequences a language allows, and English speakers have it without ever being taught it.

sections.title: Guessing the next letter reveals phonotactic knowledge
teaching: Guessing the **next letter** of a word start shows **phonotactic knowledge**. After a vowel, as in **ra_**, almost anything can follow. At the start of a word the choices narrow, to **l, r or a vowel** after sp_, b_ and f_, and to **only a vowel** after skr_ and m_.

Each item also has an impossible continuation, such as *spn, *kt, *skrl or *mb. **Guessing the next letter is predicting x₁₆**, so a **GPT** trained only on this game learns English sounds and spelling, with a flat distribution after fa_ and a sharply peaked one after skr_.

These guesses follow the rules for English syllables. What can follow a starting consonant is exactly what an English onset allows, and the impossible continuations are clusters that English never allows at the start of a syllable. Guessing well requires knowing English phonotactics.

The takeaway connects this to LLMs. **Guessing the next letter is predicting x₁₆.** A **GPT trained only on this game learns English sounds and spelling**, because its predicted distribution has to match these patterns. After fa_ its distribution is spread flat over many letters, and after skr_ it is sharply peaked on a few vowels.
